food.text: South African cuisine today is heavily based on meat, centered on braai, a social gathering where people cook meat over an open fire. Biltong, an air-dried and seasoned meat, remains a popular snack across the country.

A typical meal in a Bantu-speaking South African household is a stiff, fluffy porridge of maize meal called pap, similar to American grits, served with a flavorful stewed meat gravy. Rural families often ferment pap for a few days, giving it a tangy taste.

The rooibos variety bred by researcher Nortier became the foundation of South Africa's rooibos industry, turning production into the economic mainstay of the Clanwilliam district. In 1948 the University of Stellenbosch awarded Nortier an honorary doctorate for his contribution to South African agriculture.

By 2022, South Africa's wine industry employed 269,096 people across 536 cellars, with grapes grown by 2,613 producers. The country produced 1.13 billion liters of wine that year, and 81 percent of it was consumed domestically.

In 1994, Burke International registered the name 'Rooibos' with the US Patent and Trademark Office, giving it a monopoly there even though the plant was barely known. After losing one of the cases brought against it, Burke surrendered the name to the public domain in 2005.

For most of the twentieth century, the high-yielding Cinsaut was South Africa's most widely planted red grape, but by 2009 it made up just 2 percent of vineyards as growers shifted toward quality varieties. Cabernet Sauvignon then covered 12 percent of all plantings.

KwaZulu-Natal became one of South Africa's newest wine regions in 2005, and in July 2006 The Stables Wine Estate released the area's first Wine of Origin wine. The estate itself went bankrupt in 2012.

An outbreak of African cassava mosaic virus in Africa in the 1920s led to a major famine. The virus makes the leaves of the cassava plant wither, which limits the growth of the root. Sometime in the late 1980s a mutation in Uganda made it even more harmful, causing the complete loss of leaves. The mutated virus spread at 80 kilometres a year, and by 2005 it was found throughout Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo.

art.text: Zimbabwean art includes objects such as masks, carving, sculpture, and beadwork, used in daily life, religion, and even warfare and propaganda. In recent decades, Zimbabwe has become especially recognized around the world for its sculpture.

Although stone carving had no direct lineage to earlier tradition, its modern renaissance in Zimbabwe began only in 1954, when Frank McEwen became advisor to the new Rhodes National Gallery in Harare, serving as its founding director from 1955 to 1973. The gallery itself opened in 1957.

Since Zimbabwe's independence in 1980, Shona sculpture has continued to be exhibited in the art capitals of the world. Contemporary artists such as Dominic Benhura and Tapfuma Gutsa have won great acclaim for the art form globally.

Kingsley Sambo (1932–1977) was one of the few well-known black painters in Rhodesia before independence, having started to paint at the Cyrene Mission, where Canon Edward Paterson taught art. Two of Sambo's paintings are now held by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA).

Since 1986, Zimbabwe's National Gallery has hosted an annual exhibition of contemporary visual arts called Zimbabwe Heritage, judged by an international panel and sponsored by companies such as Mobil, Lever Brothers, and Longman. Early Award of Distinction winners in painting and graphics included Berry Bickle in 1987 and Rashid Jogee in 1992.

Frank McEwen met young artist Thomas Mukarobgwa and offered him an opportunity to pursue a career in art; Mukarobgwa became his guide to the ways of the African people. Through this connection, McEwen was introduced to sculptor Joram Mariga's early soft stone carvings, and encouraged soapstone carvers to create works reflecting their own culture.

Archaeologist Peter Garlake, born in 1934, was forced to leave Rhodesia in 1970 after his research on Great Zimbabwe was opposed by the government. Following Zimbabwean independence, he returned and spent the next ten years researching early Zimbabwean rock art.

Sculptor Bryn Taurai Mteki created a 2.5 metre sculpture called Chippi, unveiled during the sixth All-Africa Games hosted in Zimbabwe in September 1995, where it served as the games' mascot. Chippi is now displayed permanently at the National Sports Stadium in Harare beside the Games' Flame.

Bulawayo became a centre for metal sculpture in Zimbabwe, home to artists such as David Ndlovu and Adam Madebele. Arthur Azevedo, who works in Harare creating welded metal sculptures, won the President's Award of Honour at the First Mobil Zimbabwe Heritage Biennale in 1998.

Kingsley Sambo, one of the few notable black artists in Rhodesia before independence in 1980, began painting at the Cyrene Mission, where Canon Edward Paterson taught art. Two of his paintings are in the MoMA.

Sculptor Bryn Taurai Mteki, who created the 1995 Chippi sculpture for Zimbabwe's All-Africa Games, later moved to Europe. In 1996 he was honoured there with silver medals from Oelsnitz, Auerbach, and Adorf in Germany.
At the 1988 Zimbabwe Heritage exhibition, Paul Machowani won an Award of Distinction for his metal piece Ngozi. In 1992, Joseph Chanota's metal piece Thinking of the Drought won the same award.

Since 1986, the National Gallery of Zimbabwe has promoted local artists with an annual exhibition of contemporary visual arts called Zimbabwe Heritage. An international panel of judges assesses the works, and early Awards of Distinction went to Berry Bickle in 1987 and Bert Hemsteede in 1988.

war.text: The Rhodesian Bush War ran from July 1964 to December 1979 and pitted three forces against one another. They were Ian Smith's white minority-led government, Robert Mugabe's ZANLA guerrillas, and Joshua Nkomo's ZIPRA guerrillas. Neither side achieved a military victory, and a compromise was later reached.

The Rhodesian Bush War did not stay within Rhodesia's borders. It became entangled in the regional Cold War, alongside the Angolan Civil War, the Mozambican Civil War and the South African Border War, which lasted from 1966 to 1989.

In 1914, Portugal put down a Kongo revolt and abolished the titular monarchy of the Kingdom of Kongo. The title of King of Kongo was restored in 1915 and lasted until 1975, but only as an honorific without real power.

Between 1982 and 1985, the Zimbabwean military crushed armed resistance from Ndebele groups in Matabeleland and the Midlands. The campaign was called Gukurahundi, a Shona term meaning roughly 'the early rain which washes away the chaff before the spring rains'. It is also known as the Matabeleland Massacres.

In February 1981, ZIPRA guerrillas rebelled in Entumbane, a suburb of Bulawayo, barely a year after the Bush War ended. The uprising threatened to become a fresh civil war, and hundreds of people died in it. The Rhodesian African Rifles and other white-commanded ex-Rhodesian units, fighting for the new Zimbabwean government, put it down.

The Bush War ended with the Lancaster House Agreement in London in December 1979. Britain took interim direct control of the country to oversee elections in early 1980. ZANU won, and Mugabe became the first Prime Minister of Zimbabwe when independence was granted in April 1980.

The Gukurahundi was carried out by the North Korean-trained Fifth Brigade, sent to Matabeleland to crush resistance. German journalist Shari Eppel estimates about 20,000 Matabele were murdered in these first years after the war. Most of the dead were victims of public executions.

During the Entumbane uprising, ZIPRA armoured personnel carriers advanced on Bulawayo from Essexvale. Sergeant Stephen "Skippy" Devine's Eland armoured cars of the former Rhodesian Armoured Corps hit one BTR-152 with a single high-explosive anti-tank round, killing all 20 combatants inside. They then waited in the dark until two more were about 200 metres away and fired, hitting both directly and killing most of the men inside; the survivors ran off into the night. Meanwhile C and D Companies, 1RAR were pocketed by numerically superior ZIPRA fighters.

The official death toll of the Entumbane uprising was 260, though historians place it higher: Martin Meredith records "more than 300" dead, and Alexandre Binda writes that the Zimbabwe National Army units alone killed over 400 guerrillas. The Zimbabwe National Army officially reported no fatal casualties. Analysts note the irony that Mugabe and ZANU-PF were saved from a major rebellion by white-led ex-Rhodesian troops.

The Entumbane uprising was the last battle of the Rhodesian African Rifles, which was disbanded later in 1981. Its defeat prompted mass desertions by ZIPRA guerrillas who feared retribution from the Mugabe administration. It also partially fuelled Mugabe's bloody Gukurahundi campaign against Matabeleland later in the 1980s, in which the North Korean-trained 5th Brigade carried out brutal massacres and atrocities against civilians, and an estimated 10,000 to 30,000 people died.

literature.text: Tsitsi Dangarembga's Nervous Conditions, published in 1988, was the first novel in English by a Black woman from Zimbabwe. The BBC named it in 2018 as one of the top 100 books that have shaped the world.

Doris Lessing won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Literature at age 87, making her the oldest person ever to receive it. Her family had moved to Southern Rhodesia when she was a child, and she stayed there until moving to London in 1949.
The first novel in Shona was Solomon Mutswairo's Feso, published in 1957. Since then, hundreds of novels, short story collections and poetry volumes in Shona have appeared.

Feso was set several hundred years before colonization and drew on traditional Zezuru song and storytelling. It was widely read and even taught in schools until the Rhodesian government banned it in the mid-1960s.

Dangarembga wrote Nervous Conditions in 1985 but was rejected by four Zimbabwean publishers. She finally found a publisher in the London-based Women's Press, and the book won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize (Africa region) in 1989.
Lessing's first novel, The Grass Is Singing, and the short stories later collected in African Stories are set in Southern Rhodesia. She was then living there.

Poet Chirikure Chirikure performs solo or with his mbira music ensemble. His book Hakurarwi – We Shall not Sleep was chosen in 2004 as one of the 75 Best Zimbabwean Books of the 20th Century, and as one of the best five Shona publications.

Solomon Mutswairo earned his Ph.D. from Howard University in 1978 with a dissertation titled Oral Literature in Zimbabwe: An Analytico-Interpretive Approach. He also wrote the text for "Simudzai mureza weZimbabwe", the Zimbabwean national anthem.
Dangarembga's novel This Mournable Body was shortlisted for the 2020 Booker Prize, one of six novels chosen from 162 submissions. It is a sequel to The Book of Not and Nervous Conditions.

In 1982, Doris Lessing wrote two novels under the pseudonym Jane Somers to show the difficulty new authors face in getting published. Her own UK publisher rejected them, but Michael Joseph accepted them, and they appeared in 1983 and 1984.
tags: The Diary of a Good Neighbour

literature.text: In 1978, Kizito Muchemwa edited Zimbabwean Poetry in English: An Anthology, which contained only black writers' work. Using "Zimbabwean" rather than "Rhodesian" as an identity was regarded as subversive at the time, and the anthology's main theme was love of the land.

science.text: In 2006, Zimbabwe had one of the lowest life expectancies in the world according to UN figures: 44 for men and 43 for women. That was down from 60 in 1990, a fall mainly ascribed to the HIV/AIDS pandemic. The article also reports that by 1997 an estimated 25% of the population had been infected by HIV, and that deaths from starvation and disease were believed to have contributed to the population being far below what 1980 growth would have produced. By 2015 life expectancy had recovered to 60.

HIV/AIDS prevalence in Zimbabwe had been reduced to 13.5% by 2016, compared to 40% in 1998. The pandemic had earlier been the main cause of the country's sharp drop in life expectancy, and by 1997 an estimated 25% of the population had been infected by HIV in a pandemic affecting most of southern Africa.

Between 2019 and 2023, Jenfan Muswere served as Zimbabwe's minister for Postal and Courier Services and ICT. His term included the Smart Zimbabwe Master Plan for 2020 to 2030 and the National Broadband Plan for 2020 to 2030. Other achievements included the Smart Health-telemedicine initiative and the establishment of Data Centers and ICT gadget factories.
UNESCO reported that HIV prevalence among pregnant women in Zimbabwe declined from 26% in 2002 to 21% in 2004. The HIV infection rate for people aged 15–49 was estimated at 14% in 2009.

Zimbabwe's maternal mortality rate, the number of women dying per 100,000 births, was 614 in 2014, compared with 960 in 2010–11 and 232 in 1990. The under five mortality rate, the number of children dying per 1,000 births, was 75 in 2014, down from 94 in 2009.

Among Jenfan Muswere's achievements as minister were the Cyber and Data Protection Act and National Development Strategy 1, which focuses on a working Digital Economy. In 2020 he was also appointed Chairman of the Pan African Postal Union.

In 2006 an association of doctors in Zimbabwe called for Mugabe to assist the ailing health service. Infant mortality, the share of babies who died, had risen from 6% in the late 1990s to 12.3% by 2004. In late 2008 the crisis deepened, with a major cholera outbreak in December.

politics.text: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation reduced its dollar to one of the lowest valued currency units in the world. The currency was redenominated three times, and banknotes of up to $100 trillion were issued before it was effectively abandoned on 12 April 2009.

Robert Mugabe was ideologically an African nationalist. During the 1970s and 1980s he identified as a Marxist-Leninist, and from the 1990s as a socialist. He led Zimbabwe from 1980 until 2017, and critics called him a dictator. His 5th Brigade's Gukurahundi campaign in Matabeleland killed at least 20,000 people, and his later campaigns were dominated by violence and electoral fraud.

Slave raids, colonial wars and the 19th-century Scramble for Africa split the Kongo people among three colonial powers. The north went to France, the middle to Belgium and the south to Portugal. The French and Belgian regions became independent in 1960, while Angolan independence came in 1975.

In 1965, the white minority government of Southern Rhodesia under Prime Minister Ian Smith unilaterally declared independence as Rhodesia. It was responding to British demands that the colony be handed over to Black majority rule. Rhodesia then faced international sanctions and an insurgency by black nationalist organizations.
politics.source_title: History of the Jews in Zimbabwe

politics.text: The Kongo people were divided among France, Belgium and Portugal during the Scramble for Africa. In all three colonies they became one of the most active ethnic groups in the efforts to decolonize Africa, and the French and Belgian regions became independent in 1960, while Angola followed in 1975.

Manuel III Afonso, the last Manikongo, ruled as a Portuguese vassal from 1911 to 1914. He collaborated with the Portuguese, including supporting harsh contract labor. This provoked a massive anti-colonial uprising in 1913 led by Álvaro Buta, which the Portuguese crushed before abolishing the kingdom.

Mhondoro cults, centered on royal ancestral spirits in Shona traditional religion, still draw wide attendance in present-day Zimbabwe. They were instrumental in organising resistance during the First and Second Chimurengas, despite the collapse or colonial conquest of the dynasties behind them.
Roy Welensky was the second and last Prime Minister of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland. He was the son of a Lithuanian Jewish father and an Afrikaner mother.
politics.source_title: History of the Jews in Zimbabwe

politics.text: By 1915 Manuel III, previously named Manuel Martins Kiditu, had lost much of his claim to the throne. The royal family recognized Álvaro XV Afonso Nzinga as ruler instead. Manuel died of tuberculosis in 1927.

The Belgians conquered the Mwene Muji region in the early 20th century. Deadly epidemics had swept the region in the 1890s, dispersing the population. By the time the Belgians began collecting traditions, the capital Mushie appeared to be a small fishing village, and the grand claims of its ruler Muba that it once had imperial status were swept aside.

The Central African Examiner, where left-leaning white writers engaged with race, statehood and universal suffrage, ceased publication in 1965. Censorship laws put in place after Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence forced it to close.
In 1992, President Robert Mugabe upset Zimbabwe's Jewish community with a remark about white commercial farmers. He said they were hard-hearted people and that you would think they were Jews.
politics.source_title: History of the Jews in Zimbabwe

politics.text: A summary of European geographical knowledge of Africa published in 1918 placed Monemugi in modern-day Malawi. As a result, the name Monemugi was considered for the name of the modern country of Malawi.

Kikongo is the base for the Creole language Kituba, also called Kikongo ya Leta, meaning Kikongo of the state administration. The constitution of the Republic of the Congo uses the name Kituba, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo uses the term Kikongo.

philosophy.text: Kongo religion is built on a complex animistic system and a pantheon of spirits. Its Creator God is Nzambi Ampungu, the sovereign master, who gave birth to the universe. Even so, ancestor veneration is the core principle of the spirituality.

Black Consciousness grew out of the political vacuum left after the ANC and Pan Africanist Congress leaders were jailed and banned following the Sharpeville Massacre in 1960. Its roots were deeply Christian: a meeting convened by the Anglican Church in 1966 led to the University Christian Movement, which became its vehicle.

Ubuntu describes related Bantu value systems stressing that individuals are interconnected with their social and physical worlds. It is often translated as "I am because we are". The first publication devoted to ubuntu as a philosophical concept appeared in 1980, by Stanlake Samkange, who presented it as a political ideology for the new Zimbabwe.

The Black Consciousness Movement rejected what it saw as the "condescending" values of white liberals. A central tenet was the rejection of any white monopoly on truth. Although the philosophy first caused disagreement among black activists, it was soon adopted by most of them.

Steve Biko was frustrated that anti-apartheid groups such as NUSAS were dominated by white liberals. He believed they failed to comprehend the black experience and often acted in a paternalistic manner. He concluded that black people had to organise independently, and helped create the South African Students' Organisation in 1968.

Ubuntu became widely known beyond Southern Africa after South Africa's 1994 democratic transition, partly through the ubuntu theology of Desmond Tutu. Tutu chaired the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and many have argued that ubuntu was a formative influence on it.

Simon Kimbangu founded Kimbanguism in 1921 in the Belgian Congo after a mass movement began with his supposed healings and biblical teaching. The church embraces Puritan ethics, rejecting violence, polygamy, magic and witchcraft, alcohol, tobacco and dancing. Its doctrinal status for Kimbangu caused international controversy, and in 2021 the World Council of Churches discontinued the church's membership on theological grounds.

Historians John K. Thornton and Linda M. Heywood note that Central Africans have probably never agreed on the details of their cosmology. They attribute this to a process of continuous revelation and precarious priesthood. Thornton adds that missionary and colonial records of Kongo ideas were written with a hostile bias.

Biko used the word "Blacks" to include not just Bantu-speaking Africans but also Coloureds and Indians. His ideas were articulated in a series of articles published under the pseudonym Frank Talk, including a column in the SASO Newsletter.

In late August and September 1974, after holding rallies in support of the FRELIMO government in Mozambique, many Black Consciousness leaders were arrested under the Terrorism Act and the Riotous Assemblies Act, 1956, which suspended habeas corpus, so many were not formally charged until the next year. The trials that followed, including the "SASO nine" with Aubrey Mokoape and Patrick Lekota, gave members a forum to explain their philosophy and to describe the abuses that had been inflicted upon them. Far from crushing the movement, this widened its support among black and white South Africans.

In Malawi the related philosophy of uMunthu is passed on through proverbs, such as one meaning that your neighbour's child is your own and their success is yours too. Harvey Sindima treated uMunthu as an important African philosophy in his 1995 book Africa's Agenda.

Kimbangu's teachings about liberation drew working people who left their jobs to hear him speak. This threatened the colonial labor structure, so the Belgian authorities imprisoned him until his death in 1951. The church was formally recognised in 1959.

culture.text: Football is the most popular sport in Zimbabwe. The national team, the Warriors, has qualified for the Africa Cup of Nations six times, in 2004, 2006, 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2025.

Kongo religion centres on ancestor veneration, and its cosmos is split between the physical world, ku nseke, and the spiritual world, ku mpèmba. Expert healers called Banganga train extensively to commune with the ancestors and seek their guidance.

Bakongo cosmology follows the four moments of the sun, which equate with conception, birth, maturity and death. This cycle is drawn as a circle with a cross inside, called the Yowa or dikenga cosmogram, where the meeting point of the two lines is the most powerful point and where the person stands.

The Zezuru hold the Rukoto Ceremony each year to thank mhondoro, the royal ancestral spirits of Shona religion, for rainmaking. It is held at important mhondoro shrines, and sweet beer is offered to the spirits.

Zimbabwe's Jewish community, which formed in what was then Southern Rhodesia, peaked in 1961 at 7,060 people. Its numbers grew as German Jews fleeing Nazi persecution settled there in the late 1930s. Later immigrants arrived from South Africa and the United Kingdom.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Zimbabwe

culture.text: Dzivaguru is regarded as a very powerful mhondoro of the Korekore people and is believed to have ended a drought in the early 20th century. Virgin girls were given to him as wives, and he was believed to pay the bridewealth with rain.

Both Orthodox and Progressive Jewish congregations emerged in Rhodesia. The Bulawayo Progressive Jewish Congregation was founded by Rabbi Moses Cyrus Weiler in 1958. It merged with the Orthodox Bulawayo Hebrew Congregation in 1977.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Zimbabwe

culture.text: In the Kingdom of Kongo in the 20th Century, a man named Mbola is said to have died and transformed into a simbi water spirit living in a stream. He taught the living how to use his spiritual power for healing and to create sacred medicines, which became known as mbola.
